idiom_name: Razor code blocks and inline expressions in a .cshtml page (@{ }, @foreach, @Model)
implementation_notes: ASP.NET Core supplies the scriptlet structure as Razor: @{ } is a C# code block, @expression and @(expression) are inline expressions, and @foreach/@if wrap markup in control flow inside the page. C# expressions that evaluate to a string are HTML-encoded automatically and IHtmlContent is written raw, so HtmlHelper.Raw is the escape hatch that reopens the injection hole. The classic form remains justified for small internal apps and legacy .aspx maintenance; for anything maintained, hand the data to the page from a controller or page model and let the view own only markup, which is how Razor Pages and MVC are meant to be used.
pitfalls: @Html.Raw and IHtmlContent bypass encoding; using either on user-controlled text is the classic Razor XSS hole and the documentation carries an explicit warning about it.
The @model binding fails at request time: an unset or wrongly typed model produces a null-reference error mid-render, after part of the response has been written.
Statements inside a code block share the view's scope, so a page can quietly hold a DbContext or HttpClient alive for the whole render and then release it unpredictably.
Implicit expressions cannot contain generics or spaces - wrap them in @( ... ) - and text that looks like an email address in an attribute is emitted literally, so the intended value never renders.
